title: Sunrise service
hook: Protestants often gather outdoors at dawn on Easter morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, Exsultet: a fire by the door, one tall candle, and a song that kept saying this is the night. Your line was this is the night. What did one small light show you? Day one thousand thirty-five.

Folding chairs on wet grass, set out in rows facing east. A hillside, a park, a beach, a churchyard. It's cold and still mostly dark, and people are arriving in coats with blankets and thermoses, talking in low voices. A guitar is being tuned somewhere, or a little brass band is warming up. Nobody has lit a candle. They're waiting for the sun. Then, as the sky over the hill goes from gray to pink, they start to sing. Some Protestant churches gather like this on Easter morning, outdoors, timed to the dawn. Today, the sunrise service.

Why dawn? Because that's when the Gospels say the women went to the tomb, and they don't all describe the light the same way. Mark, in the King James, says they came "very early in the morning the first day of the week" and "at the rising of the sun." John says Mary Magdalene came "early, when it was yet dark." One has the sun coming up, the other has it still dark. A sunrise service sits right in that gap, in the half-light between them. Now stay with John's version, because it's built on that half-light. Mary finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She stands outside weeping. A man speaks to her, and she takes him for the gardener and asks where they've put the body. Then, in the King James: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." She doesn't know him by his face. She knows him when he says her name. Tradition traces the outdoor dawn service to Moravian Christians, and some Moravian congregations still gather in their graveyards at sunrise on Easter, among the graves, to sing. Other churches gather on hillsides, in parks, on beaches. The setting changes. The hour doesn't. People get up in the cold and stand in the dark on purpose, the way the women did, and wait for it to get light.
screen: `SHE KNOWS HIM WHEN HE SAYS HER NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a sunrise. If it's dawn where you are, go to a window that faces the light. If it isn't, turn toward the brightest window or lamp nearby, or close your eyes and remember a sunrise you've seen. Settle, and breathe. Notice how slowly the light comes: gray first, then color. Nothing about it hurries. If you pray, you can sit in the quiet the way Mary stood at the tomb, listening. If you don't, simply watch the light, or remember it, for the time. The bell holds the time.
Sunrise service. An Easter service held outdoors at dawn, at the hour the Gospels say the women came to the tomb.
Your line: early, while it was dark. Tomorrow, or the next clear morning, get up early enough to watch the sky change, even for one minute. Day one thousand thirty-five.

howItsDone: Some Protestant congregations hold an Easter sunrise service outdoors, on a hill, in a park or churchyard, with hymns and the Gospel reading of the empty tomb as the sun comes up; some Moravian congregations hold theirs in their burial grounds.

notes: Claims rule: the outline's 'Protestants often gather' is softened to 'some Protestant churches'. The Moravian origin is attributed to tradition with no date or place; 'some Moravian congregations still gather in their graveyards at sunrise' should be confirmed.
The carry ('early, while it was dark') paraphrases John 20:1 KJV 'early, when it was yet dark'; the index carry is kept exactly.
Original: ῥαββουνί (John 20:16); the Greek text transliterates an Aramaic/Hebrew word. Only John's own gloss ('Master') is given. Confirm accents.
Practice adapts 'watch a sunrise' for listeners who aren't at dawn (window, lamp, or memory).
